title: Make It Simple: -ify, -ize, -ity, -ence/-ance
objectives: I can use the suffixes -ify and -ize to understand verbs.
I can use the suffixes -ity, -ence, and -ance to understand nouns.
I can find the base word inside a longer word.
I can write about a project using precise noun and verb forms.
rationale: Suffixes turn familiar words into new words: curious into curiosity, modern into modernize, patient into patience. Students who see the pattern can decode and spell many words in science and social studies. The unit pairs four verbs that mean make (-ify, -ize) with six nouns for a state or quality (-ity, -ence, -ance), and shows the spelling changes that come with them. The passage about a school garden uses every word in a natural setting.

words.def: To make something easier to understand or do.
words.ex: Please simplify the recipe so that younger kids can follow each step.
words.ex2: The teacher simplified the long word problem by breaking it into small parts.
words.nonExample: Adding ten extra steps does not simplify a task.

morph.note: The final e of simple is dropped before -ify.

apps.academic: Scientists simplify a complex system by studying one part at a time.
apps.spoken: Can you simplify that for me? I did not follow the last part.
apps.writing: Use simplify when you rewrite or reorganize something so it is easier.

cloze.s: To ___ the long directions, Mr. Cho cut them down to three short steps.

cloze2.s: The new app helps ___ cooking by listing each step in order on one small screen.

misuse.s: The author wanted to simplify the lesson, so she added twelve confusing rules.
misuse.why: To simplify is to make something easier; adding confusing rules makes it harder.

visual.alt: A long list of directions being cut into a short list.

words.def: To remove dirt or harmful things from something.
words.ex: A filter can purify river water so that it is safe to drink.
words.ex2: The factory installed new equipment to purify the air inside the lab.
words.nonExample: Pouring mud into a clear glass does not purify the water.

morph.note: The final e of pure is dropped before -ify.

apps.academic: Many cities purify drinking water in large tanks before it reaches homes.
apps.spoken: We have to purify the stream water before we can use it for cooking.
apps.writing: Use purify for cleaning something by removing what should not be in it.

cloze.s: Boiling the stream water can help ___ it before the hikers drink.

cloze2.s: Special machines ___ the air in the hospital by trapping dust and germs.

misuse.s: The workers purify the lake by dumping oil and trash into it.
misuse.why: To purify is to clean something; dumping oil and trash makes it dirtier.

visual.alt: A water drop beside a test tube.

words.def: To make something look bigger than it is.
words.ex: A microscope can magnify a drop of pond water so students can see tiny creatures.
words.ex2: She used a lens to magnify the tiny print on the old map.
words.nonExample: Shrinking a picture to fit on a page does not magnify it.

morph.note: Magnify means make great or large; magn- is not a standalone English word.

apps.academic: A hand lens can magnify the veins of a leaf so you can count them.
apps.spoken: The mirror seems to magnify my face when I stand too close.
apps.writing: Use magnify for making an object appear larger, often with a lens.

cloze.s: The scientist used a lens to ___ the tiny wing of the fly.

cloze2.s: A hand lens can ___ the veins of a leaf so you can count each one.

misuse.s: Her glass magnified the letters by making each one much smaller.
misuse.why: To magnify is to make something look bigger; making letters smaller is the opposite.

visual.alt: A magnifying glass over an ant.

words.def: To change something to fit new ideas or tools.
words.ex: The town voted to modernize its old library with computers and a new reading room.
words.ex2: Engineers modernize bridges by adding sensors that check for cracks.
words.nonExample: Keeping an old machine exactly the same does not modernize it.

apps.academic: Factories modernize their machines to make products faster and with fewer errors.
apps.spoken: We want to modernize our club website so it works on phones.
apps.writing: Use modernize for updates that bring something in line with the present.

cloze.s: The school plans to ___ its science lab by replacing the broken equipment with new tools.

cloze2.s: Farmers hoped new machines would ___ the farm and save hours of hard work.

misuse.s: To modernize the museum, workers kept every old display exactly as it was.
misuse.why: To modernize is to update something; keeping everything the same is not modernizing.

visual.alt: An old stone building with a computer in front of it.

words.def: The state of being liked by many people.
words.ex: The game's popularity grew fast after every student tried it at recess.
words.ex2: A movie's popularity can change from one month to the next.
words.nonExample: A song that no one wants to hear has no popularity.
words.rel: nouns for a state or quality (-ity)

apps.academic: A graph can show how the popularity of a sport changed over ten years.
apps.spoken: I was surprised by the popularity of my cousin's new band.
apps.writing: Use popularity for how many people like something, often over time.

cloze.s: The ___ of the new sneakers soared, and soon every kid in class wore a pair.

cloze2.s: Because of its growing ___, the small bakery had a line out the door every morning.

misuse.s: The popularity of the song was low because every person in town loved it.
misuse.why: Popularity means being liked by many people; if everyone loves a song, its popularity is high.

words.def: A strong wish to learn or know something.
words.ex: Her curiosity led her to take apart the old radio and see how it worked.
words.ex2: The cat's curiosity got the better of it, and it climbed into the empty box.
words.nonExample: Yawning and ignoring a new puzzle shows a lack of curiosity.
words.rel: nouns for a state or quality (-ity)

apps.academic: Good scientists let their curiosity guide the questions they ask.
apps.spoken: My curiosity grew when I saw the locked door in the museum.
apps.writing: Use curiosity for the wish to find out, not for the answer itself.

cloze.s: Driven by ___, Jamal opened the strange package to see what was inside.

cloze2.s: A scientist's ___ about the stars began when she was a child with a toy telescope.

misuse.s: His curiosity made him refuse to ask any questions about how the machine worked.
misuse.why: Curiosity is a wish to learn; refusing to ask questions shows the opposite.

visual.alt: A magnifying glass beside a question mark.

words.frame: My curiosity about ___ makes me want to ___.

words.def: The quality of giving freely to others.
words.ex: The neighbor's generosity helped the family rebuild after the fire.
words.ex2: Thanks to the class's generosity, the food drive filled twelve boxes.
words.nonExample: Keeping all the snacks for yourself is not an act of generosity.
words.rel: nouns for a state or quality (-ity)

apps.academic: In many stories, a generosity that expects nothing back is the hero's best trait.
apps.spoken: Thank you for your generosity; the gift means a lot.
apps.writing: Use generosity for freely sharing time, money, or kindness.

cloze.s: The ___ of the town's people filled the shelter with blankets and food.

cloze2.s: Shira showed great ___ when she shared her whole lunch with a hungry friend.

misuse.s: Her generosity showed when she refused to share anything and kept every prize.
misuse.why: Generosity means giving freely; refusing to share is the opposite.

visual.alt: Hands holding out a wrapped gift.

words.def: The ability to wait calmly without getting upset.
words.ex: Learning to knit takes patience, because the first scarf takes weeks.
words.ex2: Dad showed patience as the slow elevator crept up to the tenth floor.
words.nonExample: Shouting after waiting only one minute shows a lack of patience.

morph.note: Patience comes from the same root as patient.

words.rel: nouns for a state or quality (-ence, -ance)

apps.academic: Scientists need patience, because experiments can take many days to show results.
apps.spoken: Thank you for your patience while I find the page.
apps.writing: Use patience for calm waiting or steady effort over time.

cloze.s: Teaching the puppy to sit took ___, since it forgot the trick every few minutes.

cloze2.s: With great ___, the fisherman waited all afternoon for one bite.

misuse.s: Her patience was clear when she shouted at the clerk after waiting only one minute.
misuse.why: Patience means waiting calmly; shouting after one minute shows impatience.

visual.alt: An hourglass beside a fishing rod.

words.def: Freedom from the control of others.
words.ex: The colonies declared their independence from Britain in 1776.
words.ex2: At ten, Ravi enjoyed his growing independence, such as walking to school alone.
words.nonExample: A child who needs help with every small task has little independence.
words.rel: nouns for a state or quality (-ence, -ance)

apps.academic: Many countries celebrate a day that marks their independence from another nation.
apps.spoken: Learning to cook gave me a sense of independence.
apps.writing: Use independence for being able to choose and act without being controlled.

cloze.s: After years of struggle, the country finally won its ___ and chose its own leaders.

cloze2.s: Learning to ride the bus alone gave Priya a feeling of ___.

misuse.s: Independence means needing someone else to make every choice for you.
misuse.why: Independence is freedom from control; needing someone else to choose is the opposite.

visual.alt: A dove flying above a bicycle.

words.def: The quality of mattering a great deal.
words.ex: The teacher explained the importance of checking your work before turning it in.
words.ex2: Doctors stress the importance of sleep for growing bodies.
words.nonExample: A tiny detail that changes nothing has little importance.

morph.note: Compare important: importance names the state of being important.

words.rel: nouns for a state or quality (-ence, -ance)

apps.academic: An author makes a reader see the importance of an idea by giving it strong evidence.
apps.spoken: I understand the importance of arriving on time.
apps.writing: Use importance for how much something matters to a person or a goal.

cloze.s: The coach spoke about the ___ of drinking water on hot days.

cloze2.s: Because of its great ___ to the town, the old bridge was repaired first.

misuse.s: She said the importance of the test was zero because it counted for half of her grade.
misuse.why: Importance is how much something matters; a test that counts for half the grade matters a lot.

passage.title: The Garden on Maple Street
paras: Ms. Alvarez's class decided to turn an empty lot on Maple Street into a garden. At first, the plan seemed too big. "Let's simplify it," said Mei. "We'll start with one bed of vegetables." Everyone agreed, and the garden club's popularity grew when other fifth graders heard about it.

Curiosity kept the students asking questions. They used a hand lens to magnify the seeds and the soil. "What is living in here?" Jonas wondered. The old well on the lot was rusty, so they asked an expert how to purify the water before using it. They also asked a builder to modernize the leaky shed with a new roof and a solar light.

The work took patience. Weeds came back after every rain, and the carrots grew slowly. But the class also gained independence: soon they could plan, plant, and water the beds without a teacher's help. Neighbors showed generosity, donating soil, seeds, and a wheelbarrow.
In June, the class carried baskets of lettuce and carrots to the food pantry. The principal talked about the importance of sharing food with others, and Mei smiled. The empty lot was no longer empty.

qs.q: In paragraph 1, the word "simplify" most nearly means
qs.why: Mei suggests starting with one bed because the plan seems too big, so simplify means make it easier.

qs.q: Which detail best shows that the students gained independence?
choices: Neighbors donated soil, seeds, and a wheelbarrow.
They could plan, plant, and water the beds without a teacher's help.
qs.why: Doing the work without help from a teacher shows freedom from control.

qs.q: Why did the garden club's popularity grow?
choices: The principal made every student join.
The garden grew food right away.
Other fifth graders heard about the club and liked the idea.
qs.why: The text says the popularity grew when other fifth graders heard about it.

qs.q: Why does the author say that the work took patience?
choices: The garden was far from school.
Weeds returned and carrots grew slowly, so the class had to keep waiting and working.
The students were tired of gardening.
qs.why: Patience is shown by steady work while waiting for slow results.

qs.q: Which statement best expresses a central idea of the passage?
choices: Students can help their community by working together with patience and generosity.
Fifth graders should always lead clubs.
Rainwater is better than well water.
qs.why: The passage follows the garden from an empty lot to a gift of food for the pantry.

teacher.overview: Students learn five suffixes (-ify, -ize, -ity, -ence, -ance) through ten words, see how verbs and abstract nouns are built from base words, and read a narrative where every unit word appears in context. The unit shows how one base word can become a verb or a noun.

notes.va.simplify.v: Simple plus -ify; the e drops. Show the word family: simple, simplify, simplicity. Ask students to simplify a sentence on the board.
notes.va.purify.v: Pure plus -ify; the e drops. Link to filters and water. Contrast purify with clean: purify removes what should not be mixed in.
notes.va.magnify.v: Magn- comes from Latin magnus, meaning great. Students will meet magnify, magnificent, and magnitude later. Use a lens or a picture.
notes.va.modernize.v: Modern plus -ize. Show -ize with organize and memorize. Ask what is modernized in their city.
notes.va.popularity.n: Popular plus -ity. Show the nouns popularity and similarity. Ask students to graph popularity of classroom favorites.
notes.va.curiosity.n: Curious changes to curios before -ity. This is a pattern for -ous words: generous becomes generosity. Practice reading the stressed syllable.
notes.va.generosity.n: Generous becomes generos before -ity. Contrast generosity with kindness: generosity involves giving something.
notes.va.patience.n: Patience and patient share a root meaning to bear or endure. Students often spell it patients; teach the difference between patience and patients.
notes.va.independence.n: In- means not, depend means rely on, -ence names the state. Ask students for a time they gained independence.
notes.va.importance.n: Importance is built on import; compare important. Students often spell -ance versus -ence by memory, so give them a short word bank to practice.

teacher.model: Think-aloud: 'The word is curiosity. I see curious at the start and -ity at the end. The e in the middle shifts to make curios- plus -ity. -ity means the state of, so curiosity is the state of being curious. A sentence: Her curiosity led her to ask questions.'
